docs.title: MSSQL Server Querier Tool
docs.text:
Article last updated: 2026-10-27.

Discovery integration recommended

This page documents a query tool. To monitor SQL Server, use Microsoft SQL Server Discovery, which is the recommended integration for this service.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
msql_query runs one SQL query against a Microsoft SQL Server database and prints the result on standard output. Pandora FMS executes it as a server plugin, so that output is the value of the module that calls it: a count, a size, a status code or any other single value a query can return.

Each run opens a connection, executes one query and exits. The command keeps no state and creates no agent. The module, its interval, its thresholds and its alerts belong to Pandora FMS; the query supplies only the value.

The addon documents two invocation forms under the same msql_query name:

  • Flag-based form. The connection and the query are passed as options (-Q, -U, -P, -H, -D). The output starts with a header line that contains the column names and continues with one tab-separated line per row. The connection selects no database, so SQL Server uses the default database of the login.
  • Positional form. The connection and the query are passed as ordered arguments. The output has no header line, and the fields of each row are joined with a delimiter, , by default.

Both forms return plain text: results go to standard output and errors go to standard error. Neither writes files, sends data to Pandora FMS by itself or returns the result in a structured format.

The Marketplace entry marks this addon as no longer actively maintained.

This page does not describe the Microsoft SQL Server Discovery addon (pandorafms.mssql), which creates agents and modules from Discovery tasks; see Microsoft SQL Server Discovery.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: Scope State Evidence Addon pandorafms.mssql_querier, version 1.0 Documented target The Marketplace package version this page describes. See Addon identity Pandora FMS NG 784 and later Supported The Marketplace states that its integrations are compatible with Pandora FMS NG 784 and later versions Network access from the Pandora FMS server to the SQL Server instance (TCP, 1433 by default) Required Both forms open a TCP connection to SQL Server. The positional form always uses port 1433 A SQL Server login allowed to run the query Required The command authenticates with the login and password you pass to it Microsoft ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server on the Pandora FMS server Required The positional form requests that driver by name An ODBC driver for SQL Server and the DBI ODBC package on the Pandora FMS server Required The flag-based form connects through DBI over ODBC Microsoft SQL Server versions Not validated No SQL Server version matrix has been recorded for this addon Operating system of the Pandora FMS server Not validated No operating system has been recorded for this version

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
1. A Pandora FMS server that can reach the SQL Server instance over the network. The command runs on the Pandora FMS server, not on the database host.
  2. A SQL Server login and password that can connect to the database and run the query you configure. No narrower permission set is published for this addon: grant the login only what the queries read.
  3. The database connectivity components required by the invocation form you use, as listed in Compatibility.
  4. The msql_query executable from the addon package, copied to the Pandora FMS server.

The command reads no configuration file and no environment variables: every setting is a command-line argument.

docs.title: Install the addon
docs.text:
Download the package from the Marketplace entry, whose download is limited to licensed users, and extract the executable. The vendor documentation calls the command msql_query.

Copy it to the Pandora FMS server and make it executable:

sudo cp msql_query /usr/share/pandora_server/util/plugin/msql_query
sudo chmod 0755 /usr/share/pandora_server/util/plugin/msql_query

Nothing has to be installed on the SQL Server host, and no agent is involved.

docs.title: Configure
docs.text:
All the configuration is a command line: the invocation form, the connection values and the query. Pandora FMS runs the command in two ways:

  • As a server plugin. Register the executable once in the console and create the module that calls it. Each run's standard output becomes the module value.
  • Manually or from a scheduler such as cron, to test the command or to obtain the value outside a console module.

docs.title: Register the command as a server plugin
docs.text:
1. Open Servers → Plugins and register a new server plugin.
  2. Set its command to the absolute path of the executable, for example /usr/share/pandora_server/util/plugin/msql_query.
  3. Write the parameters with the options of the form you use, and replace the query and the credentials with plugin fields: _field1_, _field2_, ...
-Q _field1_ -U _field2_ -P _field3_ -H _field4_
Field Description _field1_ SQL query _field2_ SQL Server login _field3_ Password for that login; mark the value as hidden _field4_ SQL Server host, including the instance when one is needed

The same registration serves every query: each module fills the fields with its own query and credentials. For the positional form, write the arguments in their order and use the fields in the same positions.

docs.title: Flag-based invocation
docs.text:
./msql_query -Q "SELECT 1 AS total" -U <USERNAME> -P <PASSWORD> -H <TARGET_HOST>
  • -Q is the query. Without it the command prints its usage summary and exits without connecting.
  • -H defaults to localhost.
  • -D sets the ODBC driver name and defaults to ODBC Driver 17 for SQL Server.
  • There is no database option: the connection selects no database and SQL Server uses the default database of the login. Qualify objects as database.schema.table when the query must read another database.
  • Options are read in pairs and their letter is not case-sensitive. An argument the command does not recognise makes it print the usage summary and exit.
  • The output contains a first line with the column names and then one tab-separated line per row.

docs.title: Positional invocation
docs.text:
./msql_query "<TARGET_HOST>" "<USERNAME>" "<PASSWORD>" "<DB_NAME>" "SELECT 1 AS total" "none"
  • The order is host, login, password, database, query, empty-result text and delimiter.
  • Six arguments are required in practice. With fewer, the command prints Not enough arguments in call. and the usage summary, although the vendor documentation marks the empty-result text as optional. Pass any value, for example none, when you do not need it.
  • The empty-result text is accepted but never printed in this version: when the query returns no rows, the command prints nothing.
  • The port is fixed at 1433. This form has no argument to change it.
  • The delimiter is , unless you pass a seventh argument. A delimiter passed as the sixth argument is read as the empty-result text and has no effect.
  • The output has no header line: each row is printed with its fields joined by the delimiter.
  • The connection sets TrustServerCertificate=yes and accepts any server certificate.

The same run with ; as the field delimiter:

./msql_query "<TARGET_HOST>" "<USERNAME>" "<PASSWORD>" "<DB_NAME>" "SELECT 1 AS total" "none" ";"

docs.title: Credentials and transport
docs.text:
• Both forms take the password as a command-line argument. It is visible in the process list while the command runs and stays in the shell history. In the console it is stored with the plugin or module definition. Use a dedicated login limited to what the queries read, and restrict who can read module definitions and who can inspect processes on the server.
  • If you invoke the command from a script or a cron entry, that file holds the password in plain text. Protect it with file permissions.
  • The connection string is assembled by concatenation: a login or a password that contains ; breaks it and the connection fails. Use credentials that do not contain that character.
  • The flag-based form passes no encryption options. Encryption and certificate validation come from the ODBC driver configuration on the Pandora FMS server.
  • The positional form always sets TrustServerCertificate=yes: the client accepts any certificate the server presents, so the connection does not authenticate the SQL Server. Use it only on a trusted network or against an instance whose identity you verify another way.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Run the form you configured manually before you rely on the module. A scalar query without table dependencies proves connectivity, authentication and output shape at once.

Flag-based form:

./msql_query -Q "SELECT 1 AS total" -U <USERNAME> -P <PASSWORD> -H <TARGET_HOST>

Expected output: the column name and then the value.

total
1

Positional form:

./msql_query "<TARGET_HOST>" "<USERNAME>" "<PASSWORD>" "<DB_NAME>" "SELECT 1 AS total" "none"

Expected output:

1

Repeat the run with a wrong password. The flag-based form prints Can't connect to <TARGET_HOST>: ... on standard error and exits with a non-zero status. The positional form prints the database driver error on standard error and exits with a non-zero status.

In the console, the module that calls the command shows the value you saw in the manual run. Confirm that the module uses the same query and the same login.

docs.title: Understand the results
docs.text:
The command returns text, and that text is the whole module value. It does not classify the result, add units or compare thresholds: thresholds, alerts and graph settings are configured on the Pandora FMS module, and the query only supplies the value they act on.

  • One value per run. A module stores one value. Write queries that return a single row and, for numeric modules, a single column. Both forms print every row the query returns, so a query with several rows produces several output lines.
  • Header line (flag-based form only). The first output line contains the column names, so a one-row result is two lines. The positional form prints only the row data.
  • Delimiter (positional form only). The fields of a row are joined with , unless you pass another delimiter. With several columns, the module value contains the joined fields.
  • Empty result. The flag-based form prints only the header line; the positional form prints nothing. The empty-result argument of the positional form has no effect.
  • NULL values. A NULL is printed as None by the positional form and as an empty field by the flag-based form. Use ISNULL() or COALESCE() in the query when a numeric module must always receive a number.
  • Exit status. A successful run exits 0. A connection or SQL error exits non-zero. An argument error prints the usage summary and exits 0, so the module can receive the usage text as its value.

docs.title: Operate and troubleshoot
docs.text:
• Every run is independent: the command connects, runs the query and exits. There is no daemon, no cache and no state to reset.
  • The command has no timeout of its own. A query that blocks keeps the execution open until SQL Server or the caller stops it. Set a timeout in the Pandora FMS plugin or module configuration when a query can run long.
  • Avoid running the command from an interactive shell with the real password when that shell records its history. Use the console module or a protected script instead.
Symptom Cause and fix The usage summary appears instead of a value (flag-based form) -Q is missing, or an argument was not recognised as an option. Check the option letters and that every option has a value. The command exits 0, so the module can store the usage text. Not enough arguments in call. or Too much arguments in call. (positional form) Fewer than six or more than seven arguments. Add the empty-result argument even when you do not need it, and remove extra arguments or join the query into one argument. Can't connect to <TARGET_HOST>: ... (flag-based form) The host, the instance, the login or the password is wrong, port 1433 is not reachable, or the instance does not accept SQL Server logins. Can't prepare statement: ... or Problem while executing: ... (flag-based form) The query is not valid for the login or for the default database. Run the same query with the same login in another SQL client. A database driver error on standard error (positional form) The connection failed or the query was rejected. The message names the driver error; check the host, the credentials, the database and the SQL syntax. A driver or data-source error from the ODBC layer The ODBC driver name does not exist on the server. Install the driver, or point -D at the exact name the server has. The module has no value The query returned no rows or only NULL values. Check the query and the data. A numeric module has no data or an unexpected value The output contains a header line, more than one row, joined columns or None. Return a single numeric scalar in a single row. The connection fails with a password that contains ; The semicolon ends the value in the connection string. Use a password without ;.

docs.title: Net usage plugin
docs.text: Article last updated: 2026-10-26.

docs.title: What it does
docs.text:
The Net usage plugin measures the traffic of the network interfaces of a Linux host and publishes it in Pandora FMS. Each run reads the kernel interface counters of the machine where it runs, adds the bytes received and transmitted by every selected interface, and writes the result as Pandora FMS module XML on standard output.

It is an agent plugin: the Pandora FMS agent runs it as one of its module_plugin lines at every agent interval and ingests the modules it prints. There is no configuration file, no credential and no network request — every figure comes from the local interface counters of the monitored host.

One run always emits one incremental module per selected interface plus one module with the total of all of them. The interface names can be narrowed with inclusion and exclusion filters, and a prefix can be added to every module name so that the same host, or several hosts in the same agent, keep their modules apart.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text:
Scope State Evidence Addon pandorafms.pandora_netusage, version 1.1 Documented target The version this page describes. See Addon identity A Linux host that exposes /proc/net/dev Required It is the only data source of the plugin: the run fails on any host that does not provide that file Rocky Linux 9 Known compatible The legacy guide for this addon records Rocky 9 as the system where it was tested. Not re-validated for version 1.1 Other Linux distributions Not validated No distribution range or version matrix has been recorded for this addon A Pandora FMS agent on the monitored host Required The plugin is executed by the agent and its output is consumed as agent plugin modules Pandora FMS versions Not validated The Marketplace carries a general banner for all its integrations, not a statement specific to this addon

The plugin runs on the monitored host itself, so it reports the interfaces of that host only. It has no remote execution mode and no connection to any other system.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
1. A Linux host with /proc/net/dev readable by the user that runs the agent. The plugin only reads that file; it needs no elevation and no other privilege.
  2. A Pandora FMS agent installed on that host and able to execute plugins. The agent is what turns the printed modules into modules in the console.
  3. A Marketplace account with a license: the download of this addon is limited to licensed users.

docs.title: Install the plugin
docs.text:
Download the package from the Marketplace entry:

https://marketplace.pandorafms.com/entries/pandorafms.pandora_netusage

The package installs the pandora_netusage executable. Copy it to the plugins directory of the agent and make it executable. With the default paths of a Linux agent that is:

cp pandora_netusage /usr/share/pandora_agent/plugins/
chmod 755 /usr/share/pandora_agent/plugins/pandora_netusage

Instead of copying the file by hand, the agent can distribute it to its hosts as a file collection; the destination is the same plugins directory.

The agent package already contains a plugin with this name

The Linux agent distribution includes its own plugins/pandora_netusage. That file is a different plugin: it publishes a single Network_Usage_Bytes module for the sum of all interfaces and accepts no options. Both files have the same name in the same directory, and the default agent configuration file already contains a module_plugin pandora_netusage line, so a copy installed under that name replaces the bundled plugin and starts running from that existing line with no options. Check that line, or install this addon under a different file name and use that name in the module_plugin line.

docs.title: Add the plugin to the agent
docs.text:
The plugin is configured in the agent configuration file (pandora_agent.conf), as one module_plugin line. The executable path is followed by the options you want to apply; the agent runs the line and ingests the module XML it prints:

module_plugin /usr/share/pandora_agent/plugins/pandora_netusage

Without options the plugin reports every interface of the host, including the loopback interface, and adds the total. Restart or reload the agent after editing the file so that the new line takes effect.

Every module_plugin line is an independent execution that produces its own set of modules. Two lines with different --module_prefix values on the same host publish two separate sets of modules, which is the way to keep, for example, one unfiltered view and one filtered view of the same interfaces.

One line, many modules

A single module_plugin line is enough for the whole host. The plugin has no option to publish one interface per module: every run emits all the selected interfaces plus the total, and the agent creates one module for each. If the default module_plugin pandora_netusage line of the agent is still in the file, the plugin runs twice per interval; with the same prefix both executions publish modules with the same names, so keep one line, or give each of them its own --module_prefix.

docs.title: Filter the interfaces
docs.text:
Two options narrow the set of interfaces. Both take a regular expression that is compared with the interface name, and both are optional:

  • --allow_regexp keeps only the interfaces whose name matches. Empty or absent, every interface is measured.
  • --deny_regexp removes the interfaces whose name matches. It is applied after the inclusion filter, so an interface matched by both is removed.

The expression is searched anywhere in the name: eth matches eth0 and veth1. Anchor it with ^ and $ to match a complete name. Names are matched as the kernel reports them, so an interface called ens192 is not matched by eth.

module_plugin /usr/share/pandora_agent/plugins/pandora_netusage --allow_regexp "^eth|^ens" --deny_regexp "^lo$"

With that line the plugin measures the eth* and ens* interfaces, leaves the loopback out, and publishes their total. Quote each pattern: the agent runs the line as a shell command, and characters such as | or $ are interpreted before the plugin receives them.

A filtered interface disappears from the plugin output, and so does its share of the total: the total is the sum of the interfaces that survive both filters. If the combination selects no interface, the run still emits the total module, with value 0.

A pattern that is not a valid regular expression is not detected when the agent starts: the run aborts with an error and prints no modules. Test the pattern manually before putting it in the agent configuration (see Verify).

docs.title: Prefix the module names
docs.text:
--module_prefix adds text in front of every module name. The prefix is concatenated with no separator, so include your own:

module_plugin /usr/share/pandora_agent/plugins/pandora_netusage --module_prefix "host01-" --allow_regexp "^eth"

That line produces host01-eth0 Network_Usage_Bytes and host01-Network_Usage_Bytes_Total. Use a prefix that identifies the host or the environment, and keep it stable: changing it creates a new set of modules and leaves the previous ones without data.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text:
Run the plugin manually from the directory that contains the executable:

./pandora_netusage --allow_regexp "^eth"

Each run executes once and exits. A successful run prints one <module> block per selected interface, in the order in which the kernel lists them, and the total block last:

<module>
    <name><![CDATA[eth0 Network_Usage_Bytes]]></name>
    <type>generic_data_inc</type>
    <data><![CDATA[4821936642]]></data>
    <description><![CDATA[Total bytes/sec transfered in this system]]></description>
    <unit><![CDATA[Bytes]]></unit>
</module>
<module>
    <name><![CDATA[Network_Usage_Bytes_Total]]></name>
    <type>generic_data_inc</type>
    <data><![CDATA[4821936642]]></data>
    <description><![CDATA[Total bytes/sec transfered in this system (all interfaces)]]></description>
    <unit><![CDATA[Bytes]]></unit>
</module>

The numbers are the cumulative counters of that moment. Run the command twice, a few seconds apart, and compare: on an interface that carries traffic the second value is larger than the first.

./pandora_netusage --help prints the usage summary, with the version and the three options.

Once the module_plugin line is in place and the agent has run it, the modules appear in the agent in the console:

To confirm what the console stores for one of them, open the module:

docs.title: Module names
docs.text:
Module name Type Unit Value <PREFIX><interface> Network_Usage_Bytes generic_data_inc Bytes Bytes received plus bytes transmitted by that interface, cumulative <PREFIX>Network_Usage_Bytes_Total generic_data_inc Bytes Sum of the previous values over the selected interfaces

<PREFIX> is the value of --module_prefix, empty by default. The interface name is followed by a space and Network_Usage_Bytes, so a host with eth0 and eth1 and no prefix produces eth0 Network_Usage_Bytes, eth1 Network_Usage_Bytes and Network_Usage_Bytes_Total.

The plugin sends no module group, no interval and no threshold: the modules are sampled at the agent interval, and any alerting or grouping is configured in the console on top of them.

docs.title: What the value means
docs.text:
Each module carries the raw kernel counter, which is what the host has accumulated since the interface came up, and the module type is incremental. Pandora FMS therefore records the growth between two consecutive samples, not the cumulative figure: an interface that has been running for weeks reports a counter in the thousands of millions, while the stored value is the traffic of the last interval. Two consecutive samples are needed before any increment exists.

The total is computed after the filters, so it always matches the interface modules of that same run. A host whose selection is empty reports a total of 0, which is the only module of that run.

There is no availability or status module. When the plugin cannot read /proc/net/dev, it prints no module at all and the existing modules simply receive no new data.

The description text of every module says Total bytes/sec transfered in this system, which describes the derived increment in the console, not the raw counter that the plugin prints.

docs.title: Everyday operation
docs.text:
• The plugin keeps no state: every execution reads the counters of that moment, so it can be run manually at any time without disturbing the agent modules.
  • The agent schedules it. Choose the agent interval according to the resolution you need: the stored increment covers the interval between two executions.
  • Interface names are part of the module names. When an interface is renamed — a new NIC naming scheme, a new virtual interface — the previous modules stop receiving data and new ones appear. Keep the filters and the prefix stable to avoid it.
  • The counters restart at zero when the host reboots or when an interface goes down and up again. The sample that follows carries a value lower than the previous one; it is not real traffic.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• No modules appear in the agent — check that the module_plugin line points to the executable that is really in the plugins directory and that the file is executable, then run it manually. Remember that the agent package contains a plugin with the same name (see Install the plugin).
  • The run prints Error: and nothing else — /proc/net/dev could not be read. Confirm that the host is Linux, that the file exists and that the agent user can read it. The message goes to standard output, and the exit status is 0, so the failure is easy to miss in a scheduled run: the agent sees a successful execution and logs nothing. Look for the message, not for the exit status.
  • The run prints no modules and reports an error about the pattern — one of the two regular expressions is not valid. Test each pattern on its own. Under the agent, a run that ends with a non-zero exit status has its output discarded and the error code logged, and the standard error of a plugin is not kept: run the command manually to read the message.
  • The total is 0 — the filters exclude every interface. Simplify --allow_regexp, or remove --deny_regexp, and run the plugin again.
  • Loopback traffic dominates the figures — the loopback interface is measured like any other. Exclude it with --deny_regexp "^lo$".
  • Modules named Network_Usage_Bytes appear instead of the documented ones — that module name belongs to the plugin bundled with the agent package, not to this addon. Check which executable the module_plugin line runs.
  • A module stopped updating after a network change — the interface name changed. Compare the module names with the current interfaces and adjust the filters.

docs.title: Command-line parameters
docs.text:
Name Required Default Description --module_prefix No Empty Text placed immediately before every module name, with no separator added. --allow_regexp No Empty (all interfaces) Regular expression searched in the interface name; only matching interfaces are measured. Anchor it with ^ and $ to match a complete name. --deny_regexp No Empty (nothing excluded) Regular expression searched in the interface name; matching interfaces are excluded. Applied after --allow_regexp, so it wins when both match. -h, --help No — Prints the usage summary, with the version and the three options, and exits.

All the options are optional and none of them takes a mandatory value. Options are given in --name value form; --name=value is also accepted.

docs.title: Generated modules
docs.text:
Module name Type Unit Description sent by the plugin <PREFIX><interface> Network_Usage_Bytes generic_data_inc Bytes Total bytes/sec transfered in this system <PREFIX>Network_Usage_Bytes_Total generic_data_inc Bytes Total bytes/sec transfered in this system (all interfaces)

The per-interface modules are emitted in the order in which /proc/net/dev lists the interfaces; the total is always the last block of the run.

docs.title: Output and exit status
docs.text: Situation Output Exit status Successful run One <module> block per selected interface and the total block, on standard output 0 --help Usage summary on standard output 0 Unknown option or malformed command line Usage error on standard error 2 /proc/net/dev cannot be read Error: followed by the command error, on standard output, and no modules 0 Invalid regular expression Error on standard error and no modules Non-zero Interrupted with Ctrl+C or SIGTERM Signal received, exiting cleanly... 0
